variants.name: Django view or service function with @transaction.atomic
variants.implementation_notes: In Django the script is a plain view, service or management-command function; @transaction.atomic (or ATOMIC_REQUESTS=True for every view) opens the transaction on entry and commits it when the function returns, rolling back when it raises, and nested atomic blocks become savepoints. The body reads as a straight line of ORM calls with no begin/commit pair, which is the closest thing to Fowler's description in Python. Flask-SQLAlchemy gives the equivalent through the session-scoped transaction. The manual form stays justified when a script must commit in stages, or when it mixes ORM calls with raw driver work - atomic() refuses explicit commit/rollback inside its block.
pitfalls: Explicit connection.commit()/rollback() or autocommit changes inside an atomic block raise TransactionManagementError - a stray call breaks the whole view.
The transaction stays open until the outermost atomic block exits, so HTTP calls and rendering inside it hold locks; Django wraps only the view, not middleware or template rendering.
With ATOMIC_REQUESTS, code that generates a streaming response runs after the view returned and therefore outside the transaction - do not write to the database there.

variants.name: Plain function with the DB-API connection context manager
variants.idiom_name: function taking a connection, transaction controlled by 'with conn:'
variants.implementation_notes: Framework-free realization: the script is a function that takes its inputs plus a connection, and the transaction boundary is the DB-API connection context manager - with conn: commits when the block exits normally and rolls back when an exception escapes (sqlite3, psycopg). This is the thinnest transaction script Python offers and the right choice for CLI tools, small services and scripts; SQLAlchemy's session.begin() context manager has the same shape over an ORM, and its Session object adds identity/unit-of-work machinery only if you want it. Remember the context manager manages the transaction, not the connection lifetime: the caller still closes the connection.
pitfalls: The sqlite3 connection context manager commits or rolls back but never closes the connection, and with autocommit=False it opens a new transaction right after committing.
Mixing the legacy isolation_level behaviour with the autocommit attribute is the classic source of 'cannot start a transaction within a transaction' errors - pick one mode.
A long-lived connection shared across threads or requests must be synchronized; sqlite3 connections are not safe to share by default.
